title: The Python GIL and its implications
prompt: What is the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) in CPython, why does it exist, and what are its practical implications for concurrent and parallel Python code?
hints: Think about what the GIL actually locks and when it is released.
Contrast threads with processes and with asyncio.
idealAnswer: The GIL is a mutex in CPython that allows only one thread to execute Python bytecode at a time, protecting CPython's memory management (especially reference counting) from race conditions without per-object locks. It exists largely for simplicity and performance of the interpreter and C extensions. Practical implications: CPU-bound multi-threaded programs cannot achieve true parallelism in CPython and may run slower than single-threaded ones; I/O-bound programs benefit from threads because the GIL is released during blocking I/O and for many C extension calls (e.g., sleeping, file reads). To get true parallelism, use multiple processes (multiprocessing, concurrent.futures.ProcessPoolExecutor) or write performance-critical work in C/Cython and release the GIL. asyncio is cooperative concurrency that sidesteps the GIL within a single thread. Alternative interpreters like Jython and IronPython historically lacked the GIL, and since Python 3.13 the GIL can be disabled via a free-threaded build.
keyPoints: GIL is a mutex allowing only one thread to run bytecode at a time in CPython
It protects interpreter internals, chiefly reference counting, and simplifies C extension memory safety
Threads are still useful for I/O-bound work because the GIL is released on blocking I/O
CPU-bound parallelism requires processes (multiprocessing) or GIL-free C extensions
asyncio offers cooperative concurrency without threads; free-threaded Python 3.13 can run without a GIL

title: Decorators
prompt: Explain what a decorator is in Python, how the syntax works, and give examples of common real-world uses of decorators.
hints: A decorator is a function that takes a function and returns a function.
Remember @decorator is syntactic sugar for func = decorator(func).
idealAnswer: A decorator is a higher-order function that takes a callable, wraps it, and returns a new callable, extending behavior without modifying the original. The @ syntax is sugar for func = decorator(func). A basic decorator is a nested function with a closure, typically using *args and **kwargs to forward arguments, and it should apply functools.wraps to preserve name and docstring. Decorators can also accept arguments by adding another layer, and classes can serve as decorators via __call__. Common uses: logging and timing functions, authentication and authorization checks, retry logic, caching (functools.lru_cache), input validation, registering functions, and measuring memory or CPU usage.
keyPoints: Decorators wrap callables to add behavior; @deco is sugar for func = deco(func)
Uses closures and *args/**kwargs forwarding
functools.wraps preserves function metadata
Decorators can take arguments (extra factory layer) and can be implemented as classes
Common uses: logging, timing, caching, auth, retries, registration

title: Generators vs iterators and yield
prompt: What is the difference between an iterator and an iterable in Python? How do generators and the yield statement work, and when would you choose a generator over a regular list?
hints: Recall the difference between __iter__/__next__ and for-loop behavior.
Generators produce values lazily, one at a time.
Think about memory for large or infinite sequences.
idealAnswer: An iterable is any object with __iter__ returning an iterator; an iterator is an object with both __iter__ (returning itself) and __next__ (returning the next element, raising StopIteration when exhausted). All generators are iterators, and range(), for example, returns an iterable that creates iterators. A generator function uses yield to pause execution, saving its full state (including local variables and the program counter), resuming on the next __next__() call; generator expressions are the compact equivalent. Generators are lazy: they compute one value at a time, so they use O(1) memory even for large or infinite sequences, they can model streams and pipelines, and they short-circuit early (e.g., stopping on first match). The trade-off is that they are single-pass and cannot be indexed or sliced, and repeated iteration requires recreating the generator; they also add a small call overhead, so for small finite data a list or tuple is simpler and faster.
keyPoints: Iterable defines __iter__; iterator defines __iter__ and __next__; generators are iterators
yield suspends the generator, preserving state across calls
Generators evaluate lazily, giving O(1) memory and support for infinite sequences
They are single-pass and not indexable
Prefer generators for large/streamed data; lists for small, reusable, indexed collections

title: list vs tuple vs set vs dict: performance and use
prompt: Compare Python's list, tuple, set, and dict. For each one, describe its characteristics, performance profile, and the situations in which you would choose it.
hints: Consider mutability, ordering, hashing, and average-case time complexity.
Tuples are immutable and can be dict keys; sets give O(1) membership.
dict lookups and set membership are hash-based, lists are linear.
idealAnswer: list is an ordered, mutable, dynamic array with O(1) append and indexing at the tail, O(n) insertions/deletions in the middle and O(n) membership tests; it is the default for ordered collections that may change. tuple is an immutable, ordered sequence with the same complexity, but because it is immutable it is hashable (when elements are hashable), smaller/faster in some cases, and safe as dict keys, function arguments, and constants. set is an unordered collection of unique, hashable elements backed by a hash table, giving average O(1) add, remove, and membership (in); it is ideal for deduplication and fast lookup, though iteration order is insertion-based in CPython but should not be relied upon. dict maps unique hashable keys to values, also hash-table-backed with average O(1) get/set; it is the standard associative container, and since Python 3.7 it preserves insertion order. Choose a list when order and mutability matter, a tuple for fixed/immutable or hashable sequences, a set for fast membership and uniqueness, and a dict for key-to-value lookups. Worst-case hash collisions can degrade to O(n), and both sets and dicts use more memory than lists/tuples.
keyPoints: list: ordered, mutable, O(1) tail ops, O(n) lookup/insert-in-middle
tuple: ordered, immutable, hashable, usable as dict keys
set: unordered, unique, hash-based O(1) membership, deduplication
dict: key->value hash table, O(1) get/set, insertion-ordered since 3.7
Memory: list/tuple compact; set/dict heavier due to hashing

title: Duck typing vs static typing and PEP 484 type hints
prompt: What is duck typing in Python, how does it relate to the EAFP style, and what role do PEP 484 type hints and tools like mypy play? Discuss the trade-offs of dynamic vs static typing.
hints: Duck typing: 'if it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck'.
Type hints are optional annotations checked by external tools, not at runtime.
Contrast flexibility and iteration speed with safety and maintainability.
idealAnswer: Duck typing means an object's suitability is determined by the presence of methods and attributes rather than by its declared type; if it quacks, treat it as a duck. Python uses this together with EAFP (Easier to Ask for Forgiveness than Permission): try to use the interface and catch AttributeError/TypeError rather than checking types upfront. Protocols (typing.Protocol, structural subtyping) formalize duck typing for type checkers. PEP 484 introduced optional type hints, which are metadata the interpreter largely ignores; static checkers like mypy, pyright, and the built-in type comments, plus IDE autocomplete, validate them. Trade-offs: dynamic typing and duck typing give flexible, concise code, fast prototyping, and easy interoperability, at the cost of runtime type errors, weaker IDE support, and harder maintenance in large codebases. Static typing improves correctness, refactoring safety, self-documentation, and performance of compiled implementations (e.g., mypyc, PyPy), but adds verbosity and overhead and can feel restrictive for quick scripts. The pragmatic approach is gradual typing: use hints on public APIs and hot paths, and keep duck typing for internal flexible code.
keyPoints: Duck typing relies on capabilities (methods/attributes) rather than declared types
EAFP complements it: attempt the operation and catch exceptions
PEP 484 type hints are optional and checked statically, not at runtime
mypy/pyright catch type errors before execution and power IDE features
Gradual typing balances dynamic flexibility with static safety
